# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure worldwide [1]. For decades, neurohormonal blockade with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) formed the cornerstone of treatment for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [2]. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift by simultaneously augmenting beneficial natriuretic peptide systems while inhibiting the deleterious effects of the RAS [3].

## Pharmacology and Rationale

Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [4]. Inhibition of neprilysin increases circulating natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of pathologic remodeling and fibrosis [5]. Because neprilysin inhibition alone also raises angiotensin II, concurrent angiotensin receptor blockade is required to realize clinical benefit [6]. An earlier strategy combining neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) was abandoned owing to an unacceptable rate of angioedema attributed to dual bradykinin potentiation [7]. Sacubitril/valsartan, a supramolecular sodium salt complex, circumvented this problem by pairing the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with valsartan rather than an ACE inhibitor [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Trial Evidence

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8,442 patients with NYHA class II–IV HFrEF to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [9]. The trial was stopped early because of overwhelming benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, with significant reductions in all-cause mortality [9]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progressive pump failure, as well as improvements in quality of life and symptoms [10,11]. Benefit was consistent across subgroups, including the elderly and those with diabetes [12,13]. The TITRATION study established that gradual up-titration improved tolerability, particularly regarding hypotension [14].

In HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial narrowly missed its primary endpoint, with a rate ratio of 0.87 (P=0.06) for total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [15]. Prespecified analyses suggested potential benefit in patients with ejection fraction below the normal range and in women, prompting interest in the role of ARNI across the ejection fraction spectrum [16,17].

The PIONEER-HF trial demonstrated that in-hospital initiation among patients stabilized after acute decompensated HF was safe and produced greater reductions in NT-proBNP than enalapril [18]. The TRANSITION study similarly confirmed feasibility of early initiation [19]. The PROVE-HF study linked NT-proBNP reduction with favorable reverse cardiac remodeling, including improvements in ejection fraction and left atrial and ventricular volumes [20].

## Mechanistic and Biomarker Insights

ARNI therapy lowers NT-proBNP while raising BNP, reflecting neprilysin's role in BNP degradation; thus NT-proBNP is the preferred monitoring biomarker [21]. Beneficial effects on cardiac fibrosis biomarkers and on atrial remodeling have been reported [22]. Effects on renal function appear favorable, with slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate compared with enalapril despite modest increases in albuminuria [23].

## Safety and Tolerability

The principal adverse effects are hypotension and, less commonly, hyperkalemia and renal dysfunction [9]. Angioedema occurred infrequently but mandates a 36-hour washout when transitioning from an ACE inhibitor [24]. A pharmacovigilance interest in possible effects on amyloid-beta clearance, given neprilysin's role in its degradation, prompted the PERSPECTIVE cognitive study, which did not show cognitive harm [25].

## Guidelines and Practical Implementation

Contemporary guidelines from the American and European societies recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy for HFrEF, either replacing an ACE inhibitor/ARB or as initial neurohormonal therapy [26,27]. ARNI is now considered one of the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy alongside beta-blockers, MRAs, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [28]. Despite robust evidence, real-world uptake has been suboptimal, attributed to cost, clinical inertia, and concerns about hypotension [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses generally support its value in HFrEF, though affordability remains a barrier in many settings [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF, delivering substantial reductions in mortality and hospitalization and facilitating reverse remodeling [9,20]. Its role in HFpEF is more nuanced, with benefit concentrated in patients at the lower end of the preserved ejection fraction range [15,16]. Early in-hospital initiation is safe and effective [18]. Future efforts should focus on improving implementation, addressing cost barriers, and clarifying the optimal patient populations across the ejection fraction continuum.
